Relative Clauses: Prepositions and Relative Clauses After Pronouns

Remember: Relative Clauses are clauses (sentences) that start with relative pronouns who, that, which, whose, where, and when.
There are rules about using prepositions in relative clauses and using relative clauses after pronouns.

Relative Clauses are used to clarify which person or thing we are talking about.
Examples:
This is the man who helped me during the project.
The dogs that love cats are special.
The beach was definitely the thing which I enjoyed most about my holiday.
I met a girl whose husband is a pilot.
This is the company where I worked for 20 years.
I remember my graduation party. It was the day when the earthquake happened.
As you can see, those relative pronouns provide extra or specific information about the people or things we are talking about.

When a preposition is needed in a relative clause, it can be placed before the relative pronoun or at the end of the clause.

For example:
Science is a subject which I always had trouble with.
Science is a subject with which I always had trouble. (This structure is generally more formal)

There are some fixed prepositional phrases you can use in non-defining relative clauses such as:</br><span class="italic"> in which case </br>at which point</br> as a result of which</br> the result of which was that</br> by which time

For example:
It was a massive scandal, as a result of which every single employee resigned.

Defining relative clauses usually come after these pronouns:

something, anything, nothing, everything, someone, anyone, many, all, those, some, little, much

For example:
Many who saw the movie were amazed.

Body Language in the Workplace
Did you know that 95% of communication is non-verbal? This means that your body language has a great impact on the way people perceive you.

Having excellent non-verbal communication skills tells your audience (whether they be a group of people at a presentation, or an individual coworker) that you are confident, honest and motivated.  </br></br>Here are a few things to keep in mind about your body language at work:

1. Posture - how you feel affects how you stand. Stand tall, with your shoulders back and head up.
  2. Be in sync with others around you. Observe their body language and try to match it. That makes you appear interested and engaged.
  3. Eye contact. Being able to maintain eye contact with someone communicates confidence, authority and attentiveness.
  4. Show interest. Respond verbally and nonverbally to what others are saying.
  5. Try not to fidget. Fidgeting is interpreted as a nervous habit and most people are unaware they do it.

images.text:
When you are making a presentation, you need to observe your audience. This is to help you gauge their level of interest. If you have an idea of what gets their attention, you will not only be able to get a good idea of how engaging your content is, but you will also connect better with them. Intuitively, people pick up on the small movements and gestures known as body language in which case,
you need to be aware of the following: </br></br>

Facial Expressions
These are fairly self-explanatory. You might not always have a clear view of the audience's faces, but facial expressions can be extremely useful to determine audience reactions.

Leaning Forward
Leaning forward toward the person who is presenting is often subconscious. It is a typical indicator of interest whereas leaning back may indicate that someone is bored.

Crossing of Arms
Most people think that this is a defensive signal which likely indicates a difference of opinion. It could be that an audience member is reacting in this way because they find the subject sensitive or that they are not satisfied with something that has been said.

It is worth your while to note that an audience member who exhibits this body language may not be giving off either of these subconscious signals. If someone sits with arms crossed for the duration of the presentation, it doesn't necessarily mean they are upset or angry by what you are saying. It might be that sitting in this way, they are in their comfort mode. Similarly, if a person keeps shifting around in their chair because they want to get comfortable, it might not mean they are bored or restless.
If you have the chance to observe the behavior of the whole group rather than each individual, you will get a more precise idea of the general audience response to your presentation.
